domain: Assaying and hallmarking — the guild-regulated metrology of precious metals: touchstone streak tests, cupellation, millesimal fineness, statutory sampling, assay-office and date-letter punches, and the defacement of substandard work.
axioms: A mark certifies exactly one tested property of one sampled portion; it says nothing about weight, workmanship, provenance, or worth, and every reliance beyond that property is unsecured.
Cheap surface tests and definitive destructive tests catch different frauds; a regime that runs only the cheap test passes anything shaped correctly on the surface.
The hardest fraud is not a forged mark but a genuine mark transposed onto a different object — correctly-formed evidence attached to the wrong body.
An assay is a sample; a sample certifies a batch only when the sampling rule is stated and the batch is homogeneous.
A mark that functions as a toll creates an evasion economy: makers reroute around the threshold rather than meet it, and the cheapest route is the one that gets taken.
A certification is worthless unless it records who struck it, when, and against which standard was then in force.
One number summarising a mixture (fineness over an alloy) hides which constituent is missing; consumers of the number cannot recover what the assay merged.
primitives: the sampled portion versus the whole object
fineness expressed as a single millesimal number
the punch, the struck mark, and its transposition
assay-office mark and date letter (who certified, when)
the standard in force at the moment of marking
the weight/type threshold that triggers compulsory assay
defacement or rejection of substandard work
the downstream buyer who relies on the mark without re-testing
failure_mode: Reasons one object at a time and has no vocabulary for aggregate throughput or backlog — it will not notice that 81 objects were never submitted for assay at all.
Sees certification integrity as the question and can miss that the certification regime itself may be unnecessary for this object; it hardens a gate rather than asking whether the gate should exist.

Assumes an independent certifier and a stable, externally-set standard; poorly calibrated for a format expected to change under its own users, or where the maker, the warden, and the buyer are the same person.
Conservative bias: treats any relaxation of a check as new fraud surface, over-weighting adversarial cases in a single-operator estate where nobody is trying to cheat.
Indifferent to the cost of the test on the human performing it — cupellation destroys the sample and the warden does not care how long it took.
